The provider block names the account ID, the API host and the token ([provider configuration](https://github.com/dbt-labs/terraform-provider-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.1/docs/index.md#L44-L54)). Your dbt models live in Git. The dbt Cloud objects say where, how and when those models run. Terraform manages these run settings, not the models.

The objects sit at two levels ([Account and Project](#account-and-project-account-and-project)):

- The account holds objects that many projects share, such as global connections to a data platform, service tokens and user groups.
- A project holds a Git repository, credentials, environments, environment variables and jobs.

Inside a project, two objects do most of the work:

- An environment decides where and how the code runs: the connection, the credential, the dbt version and the Git branch ([The Environment Decides Where](#the-environment-decides-where-the-environment-decides-where)).
- A job decides what runs and when: the dbt commands, the triggers and the target name. Each job belongs to one environment.

Three more ideas explain most plans. The type of an environment switches dbt features on and off ([Environment Types Are Switches](#environment-types-are-switches-environment-types-are-switches)). account-and-project.wrapped_text:
Account and Project
A global connection,
`dbtcloud_global_connection`, belongs to the
account and holds the details of one data
platform, such as a Snowflake account. A
project does not point to a connection. Each
environment of the project does, with
`connection_id` ([environment doc](https://git
hub.com/dbt-labs/terraform-provider-dbtcloud/b
lob/v1.13.1/docs/resources/environment.md#L72)
). So one connection can serve many projects.

A project holds the rest:

- `dbtcloud_repository` names the Git
repository. `dbtcloud_project_repository`
links it to the project.
- A credential, such as
`dbtcloud_snowflake_credential`, holds the
user, role, schema and secret that one
deployment environment uses.
- `dbtcloud_environment` combines a
connection, a credential and code settings.
- `dbtcloud_environment_variable` holds one
variable with a value for each environment.
- `dbtcloud_job` holds the commands that run
in one environment.

Provider version 1.0.0 removed the older
connection resources, such as
`dbtcloud_connection` and
`dbtcloud_project_connection`.
`dbtcloud_global_connection` replaces them
([upgrade guide](https://github.com/dbt-labs/t
erraform-provider-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.1/docs/g
uides/90_upgrading_from_v0_to_v1.md#L7-L12)).

the-environment-decides-where.wrapped_text:
The Environment Decides Where
An environment is either `development` or
`deployment`. A project has one development
environment and as many deployment
environments as needed ([environment doc](http
s://github.com/dbt-labs/terraform-provider-dbt
cloud/blob/v1.13.1/docs/resources/environment.
md#L11)). Each environment sets four things ([
arguments](https://github.com/dbt-labs/terrafo
rm-provider-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.1/docs/resourc
es/environment.md#L72-L83)):

- `connection_id`: the data platform.
- `credential_id`: the identity for deployment
runs. A development environment has none,
because each developer sets their own
credentials in dbt Cloud.
- `dbt_version`: for example `latest` or
`versionless`.
- `custom_branch`: the Git branch to run.

A job adds what to run and when:
`execute_steps` holds the dbt commands,
`triggers` holds the trigger flags, and
`target_name` sets the value of `target.name`
in the models ([job doc](https://github.com/db
t-labs/terraform-provider-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.
1/docs/resources/job.md#L216-L246)). A model
that checks `target.name` therefore behaves
according to the job, not the environment.

environment-types-are-switches.wrapped_text:
Environment Types Are Switches
A deployment environment has a
`deployment_type`: `production`, `staging`, or
empty for a general environment ([environment 
doc](https://github.com/dbt-labs/terraform-pro
vider-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.1/docs/resources/env
ironment.md#L76)). The value is more than a
label. dbt uses it to decide how references
between projects resolve in dbt Mesh, and it
sets the variable `DBT_CLOUD_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE`
in each run ([project dependencies](https://do
cs.getdbt.com/docs/mesh/govern/project-depende
ncies); [special variables](https://docs.getdb
t.com/docs/build/environment-variables)). That
variable is `prod`, `staging`, or empty for a
general environment.

The environment `type`, development or
deployment, cannot change in place. A new
value replaces the environment ([schema](https
://github.com/dbt-labs/terraform-provider-dbtc
loud/blob/v1.13.1/pkg/framework/objects/enviro
nment/schema.go#L234-L240)), and the pitfall
Replacements Delete Jobs shows what follows.

what-the-provider-reads-back.wrapped_text:
What the Provider Reads Back
A refresh reads most settings of jobs and
environments from dbt Cloud. So an edit in the
dbt Cloud UI to such a setting shows in the
next plan, and the apply reverts it. The
[Terraform map](../terraform.md#outside-change
s-get-reverted-outside-changes-get-reverted)
shows the same effect with Snowflake.

Secrets are the exception. The dbt Cloud API
masks them, so the provider cannot read them
back. For an environment variable whose name
starts with `DBT_ENV_SECRET`, the provider
keeps the values from its own state
([environment variable code](https://github.co
m/dbt-labs/terraform-provider-dbtcloud/blob/v1
.13.1/pkg/framework/objects/environment_variab
le/resource.go#L161-L182)). A secret that
someone changes in the UI therefore never
shows in a plan, and the next apply does not
restore it either.

two-provider-generations.wrapped_text:
Two Provider Generations
Provider 1.0.0 rewrote the provider on
HashiCorp's newer Plugin Framework. It changed
the schema of several resources and removed
the old connection resources ([upgrade guide](
https://github.com/dbt-labs/terraform-provider
-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.1/docs/guides/90_upgradin
g_from_v0_to_v1.md)). The Terraform Registry
shows the docs of the latest version by
default. A configuration pinned to 0.x needs
the 0.x docs, which GitHub keeps under the
tag, for example [v0.3.26](https://github.com/
dbt-labs/terraform-provider-dbtcloud/tree/v0.3
.26/docs).

Some arguments still exist but are deprecated:

- `triggers.custom_branch_only`: the docs say
to remove it; jobs now use the environment's
branch ([job doc](https://github.com/dbt-labs/
terraform-provider-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.1/docs/
resources/job.md#L216)).
- `timeout_seconds` on a job: use
`execution.timeout_seconds` instead ([job doc]
(https://github.com/dbt-labs/terraform-provide
r-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.1/docs/resources/job.md#
L244)).
- `deferring_job_id`: use
`deferring_environment_id` instead ([job doc](
https://github.com/dbt-labs/terraform-provider
-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.1/docs/resources/job.md#L
14)).

| Resource | dbt Cloud object | What to check
| Import ID |

`credential_id`, `dbt_version` |
`project_id:environment_id` |

dbtcloud-where-to-look-first.wrapped_text:
Where to Look First
Read a dbt Cloud configuration in this order:

1. `required_providers` and the lock file. A
0.x pin means the Registry docs do not match;
read the docs at the pinned tag.
2. The `provider "dbtcloud"` block. Check
`host_url` and where the token comes from.
3. The backend and the workspaces. Find which
environments share one state, because one plan
then touches all of them.
4. `dbtcloud_project`, and the `import` and
`moved` blocks. They show which objects were
first made in the UI.
5. The connection, or the data source that
finds it, and the `connection_id` of every
environment.
6. The environments: `type`,
`deployment_type`, the credential wiring,
`dbt_version` and the branch.
7. The credentials: `auth_type`, the Snowflake
names, and where the private key comes from.
8. The jobs: `execute_steps`, `target_name`,
`triggers`, the schedule fields and
`num_threads`.
9. The environment variables, and which values
are secret.
10. The outputs and pipelines that use job
IDs, and the Snowflake code that creates the
named database, role and warehouse.

dbtcloud-plan-signals.wrapped_text:
Plan Signals
| Line in the plan | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `~ triggers` or `~ schedule_*` on a job
without a code change | Someone changed the
job in the UI; the apply will revert it. |
| `-/+ dbtcloud_environment` | The environment
is replaced; dbt deletes its jobs with it. |
| `-/+ dbtcloud_job ... triggers` | The job
changes type between CI, merge and other jobs;
it gets a new ID. |
| `+ credential_id = (known after apply)`
right after an upgrade to 1.x | The new
version stores empty values as null instead of
0 ([issue 519](https://github.com/dbt-labs/ter
raform-provider-dbtcloud/issues/519)). |
| `target_name = "default"` on a new job | The
job uses the provider default; models that
check `target.name` may skip production logic.
|

ui-edits-get-reverted.wrapped_text:
UI Edits Get Reverted
dbt Cloud lets anyone with the right role edit
a job in the UI. When the job is in Terraform,
the next apply reverts that edit, with no
warning beyond the plan line. dbt Cloud keeps
the settings history of each job for 90 days,
so you can see what changed ([deploy jobs](htt
ps://docs.getdbt.com/docs/deploy/deploy-jobs))
. Make every change to a Terraform-managed job
in code.

`sensitive` only hides them in plan output

terraform-provider-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.1/docs/

values of environment variables are not even

Secrets in State and Out of Sight
The private key and passphrase of a credential are stored in the state in plain text; `sensitive` only hides them in plan output ([credential doc](https://github.com/dbt-labs/terraform-provider-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.1/docs/resources/snowflake_credential.md#L62)). The values of environment variables are not even marked sensitive ([variable doc](https://github.com/dbt-labs/terraform-provider-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.1/docs/resources/environment_variable.md#L39)). Newer 1.x versions add write-only arguments such as `private_key_wo`, which keep a secret out of the state; they need Terraform 1.11 or later ([credential doc](https://github.com/dbt-labs/terraform-provider-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.1/docs/resources/snowflake_credential.md#L26-L27)). And a secret changed in the UI stays invisible to Terraform, as What the Provider Reads Back explains.

lookups-by-name.wrapped_text:
Lookups by Name
A configuration can find a global connection
by its name, with the data source
`dbtcloud_global_connections` and a filter. If
someone renames the connection, the lookup
returns nothing and the environment create
fails. Two connections can also share one
name; the provider's changelog suggests a
check that names do not repeat ([changelog](ht
tps://github.com/dbt-labs/terraform-provider-d
btcloud/blob/v0.3.26/CHANGELOG.md#L118-L121)).
Pass the connection ID from the state that
owns the connection, or keep both in one
state.

Replacement Pitfalls
These pitfalls delete jobs or change their
IDs.
dbtcloud-replacement-pitfalls.wrapped_original_text:
Replacement Pitfalls
These pitfalls delete jobs or change their IDs.

replacements-delete-jobs.wrapped_text:
Replacements Delete Jobs
dbt deletes an environment's jobs together
with the environment ([delete an environment](
https://docs.getdbt.com/faqs/Environments/dele
te-environment-job)). So a plan that replaces
an environment, for example after a change of
`type`, also takes its jobs with it. A job
also gets a new ID when its triggers move it
between kinds: CI, merge, or other ([job code]
(https://github.com/dbt-labs/terraform-provide
r-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.1/pkg/framework/objects/
job/resource.go#L128-L157)). Any pipeline or
service that starts the job by ID then calls a
job that no longer exists.

Setting is_active to False Deletes the Job
`is_active = false` sounds like a pause, but
the docs say it "is the same as creating a job
in a deleted state" ([job doc](https://github.

v1.13.1/docs/resources/job.md#L230)). To pause
a job, set every trigger to `false` instead ([
triggers](https://github.com/dbt-labs/terrafor
m-provider-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.1/docs/resource
s/job.md#L216)).

Authoritative Group Lists
`dbtcloud_user_groups` owns the full list of
groups of a user. It removes any group that
someone added in the UI ([user groups doc](htt

tcloud/blob/v1.13.1/docs/resources/user_groups
.md#L17)). A team that manages some groups in
code and others by hand loses the hand-made
ones at the next apply.

Job Setting Pitfalls
These pitfalls come from defaults that
differ from the UI.
dbtcloud-job-setting-pitfalls.wrapped_original_text:
Job Setting Pitfalls
These pitfalls come from defaults that differ from the UI.

job-defaults-differ.wrapped_text:
Job Defaults Differ from the UI
The provider has its own defaults for two job
settings ([job schema](https://github.com/dbt-
labs/terraform-provider-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.1/
pkg/framework/objects/job/schema.go#L541-L553)
):

- `target_name` defaults to `"default"`. A
macro or model that runs only when
`target.name == 'prod'` silently skips that
logic.
- `num_threads` defaults to 1. The UI suggests
4 threads ([deploy jobs](https://docs.getdbt.c
om/docs/deploy/deploy-jobs)), so a Terraform
job without the setting runs one model at a
time.

Set both on every job.

jobs-started-by-api.wrapped_text:
Jobs Started by the API
A job with all triggers off runs only when
something calls the API. The scheduler queues
such runs, and it does not cancel
over-scheduled runs that the API started ([job
scheduler](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/deploy
/job-scheduler)). A slow job that a pipeline
calls every hour can therefore build a growing
queue. dbt also deactivates a job after 100
failed runs in a row. A successful call to
start a run says nothing about the result; the
caller must poll the run.

version-gap.wrapped_text:
Version Gap
A constraint such as `~> 0.3` with no
committed lock file stays on 0.3.26, the last
0.x release. The Registry docs then describe a
different schema. An upgrade to 1.x needs
care: the first 1.x plans can show
`connection_id` and `credential_id` changes
([issue 429](https://github.com/dbt-labs/terra
form-provider-dbtcloud/issues/429); [issue 519
](https://github.com/dbt-labs/terraform-provid
er-dbtcloud/issues/519)). Read the upgrade
guide and the changelog, upgrade in one step
to a recent 1.x version, and review the first
plan line by line.

who-schedules-the-jobs.wrapped_text:
Who Schedules the Jobs
dbt Cloud can start jobs on a schedule, on a
merge, or on a pull request. A team can
instead turn all triggers off and start jobs
from its own orchestrator through the API. The
second way gives one scheduler for all systems
and quiet plans. Its costs: the dbt Cloud UI
shows no schedule, runs can queue (see Jobs
Started by the API), and the orchestrator must
poll each run for its result.

import-what-the-ui-built.wrapped_text:
Import What the UI Built
Many dbt Cloud accounts start in the UI.
`import` blocks adopt those objects without a
destroy, and `moved` blocks keep them safe
during refactors. dbt Labs offers the tool
`dbtcloud-terraforming`, which writes both the
configuration and the import blocks for an
account ([import guide](https://github.com/dbt
-labs/terraform-provider-dbtcloud/blob/v1.13.1
/docs/guides/3_importing_existing_configuratio
n.md#L8-L10)).

key-pairs-for-snowflake.wrapped_text:
Key Pairs for Snowflake
dbt Cloud no longer lets you create Snowflake
credentials with a user name and password. New
credentials default to key pairs, and dbt
recommends PKCS#8 keys ([connect Snowflake](ht
tps://docs.getdbt.com/docs/platform/connect-da
ta-platform/connect-snowflake)). In Terraform,
pass the key from a secret file at run time,
and use `private_key_wo` on Terraform 1.11 or
later, so the key stays out of the state. The
[authentication map](../../authentication/auth
entication.md#private-key-private-key)
explains key-pair sign-in.

leave-some-objects-out.wrapped_text:
Leave Some Objects Out
Not every dbt Cloud object belongs in
Terraform. Two examples:

- Any change to a service token replaces it,
because the API does not allow changes to an
existing token. The new token has a new secret
([changelog](https://github.com/dbt-labs/terra
form-provider-dbtcloud/blob/v0.3.26/CHANGELOG.
md#L17)).
- `dbtcloud_user_groups` removes groups that
people add by hand (see Authoritative Group
Lists).

Objects that people change often, or whose
replacement breaks callers, can stay in the
UI. Write down which objects Terraform owns.
